paras: The lynching of Henry Solomon took place at the Bossier parish jail in Bellevue, Louisiana, in the early hours of January 25, 1882, when ten or twelve unknown men took the jail keys from a deputy sheriff and hanged Solomon, a Black prisoner held on a charge of mule stealing. Hours earlier, by the deputy's account, Solomon had set his cell on fire in an attempt to escape. A coroner's jury found that he died by hanging at the hands of 'parties unknown,' and a Louisiana editor later held up the case as evidence that lynchers spared white criminals.

Solomon was confined at Bellevue on a charge of stealing a mule from John J. Stockwell. On the night of January 10 he broke jail with Jack Chapman, a prisoner under sentence of death for murder. According to the Shreveport Times, Deputy Sheriff John C. Elstner found Solomon hiding in a closet at a house near the Shreveport depot, and a Bossier deputy brought him back to Bellevue. The Bossier Banner wrote that he was 'of a bad character' and that his re-arrest had been instigated and paid for by Black people on his own plantation, a claim it attributed to the evidence and to the coroner.

About 10:30 on the night of Tuesday, January 24, deputy sheriff R. E. Wyche Jr. discovered a fire in the upper west cell, where Solomon was held alone, shackled and chained to the floor. Wyche testified that Solomon had broken his chain and admitted setting the fire to escape, and that deputies and townspeople put it out before the building was lost. He was afterward moved to the upper east cell, which he shared with Chapman.

Between 1 and 2 a.m., ten or twelve men entered the room at his father's house where Wyche was sleeping with deputy C. W. Edwards and two Black men, Thomas Paysinger and Sledge Bryant, and compelled him by threats to hand over the keys. Wyche said the men gave him 'no time to parley' and did not say what they meant to do. In the morning Solomon was found hanging dead by a rope from the jail scaffold, a spot the Shreveport wire placed at the second story of the jail and the Donaldsonville Chief 'just outside the building.'

An inquest before parish coroner Dr. W. J. Mobley returned a verdict of death by dislocation of the neck caused by hanging 'by the hands of parties unknown.' Edwards, Paysinger and Bryant corroborated Wyche, and two prisoners, Knight Pitts and Robert Rump Jr., testified that they had been asleep and knew nothing of the hanging. No report of arrests or of a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Bossier Banner, published at Bellevue, printed the inquest testimony under the headline 'Arson and Judge Lynch.' It called the method 'undoubtedly dangerous' and hoped never again to report 'Judge Lynch in our midst,' but blamed 'the legal quibbles and quirks so freely used in defence of criminals.' A Shreveport dispatch dated January 26 ran the next day in the Savannah Morning News as 'Judge Lynch in Louisiana. A Horse Thief and Incendiary Hanged,' in the Richmond Dispatch as 'Louisiana Lynch Law,' and in the Knoxville Daily Chronicle as 'A Negro Hanged.' The Claiborne Guardian at Homer gave a short factual account on February 1.

The sharpest response came from the Donaldsonville Chief, whose editorial 'More Lynching' said Bossier had been 'disgraced' and called the lynchers 'night-prowling jayhawkers' and 'cowardly murderers.' The Chief rejected the Banner's excuse, noting that Solomon had never been tried, and argued that the mob had passed over Chapman, whom it called 'a white man' convicted of murder, making 'a very marked distinction between white tweedle-dee and colored tweedle-dum.' Later reports in the Banner and the Washington Evening Star described Chapman as 'colored.'

The French-language Opelousas Courier reported that Solomon, 'in despair,' hanged himself the same evening as the fire, a version contradicted by the sworn inquest testimony and the coroner's verdict. Sources also differ on the charge (mule stealing locally, horse stealing in the wire) and on the date: Wyche's printed testimony gives January 26 for the taking of the keys, while the Banner's narrative and the wire place the discovery of the body on the morning of January 25.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Solomon
bases: Ten or twelve unknown men took the jail keys from a deputy by threats, removed Henry Solomon from his cell and hanged him at the Bossier parish jail; the coroner's jury found death by hanging 'by the hands of parties unknown' (A2, A3, A10).

A group of 10 or 12 men without lawful authority forced the jail keys from a deputy and hanged a Black prisoner held on a mule-stealing charge who had just set the jail afire (A2, A3); the local paper and the wire both called it 'Judge Lynch' and the Donaldsonville Chief said the lynchers acted 'under the pretense of punishing crime' (A6, A10). One French-language brief says he hanged himself (A11), against the coroner's verdict.

The local Bossier Banner with the coroner's inquest, the Shreveport wire and the Claiborne Guardian agree that unknown men hanged Solomon (A2, A6, A9), but the Opelousas Courier brief says he hanged himself (A11), a secondhand report contradicted by the sworn inquest testimony (A2, A3).

accounts.label: Coroner's inquest and deputy's testimony
accounts.gist: Solomon set his cell afire about 10:30 p.m. and admitted doing so to escape; between 1 and 2 a.m. 10 or 12 unknown men forced the keys from deputy Wyche, and Solomon was found hanged from the jail scaffold; the jury found death by hanging by parties unknown.

accounts.label: Shreveport wire
accounts.gist: A Black prisoner held for horse stealing set fire to the jail about midnight and was found the next morning hanging from the second story; there was no clue to the hangers.

accounts.label: Opelousas Courier brief
accounts.gist: After his attempt to burn the jail on the night of the 24th failed, Solomon, in despair, hanged himself the same evening.

framing.detail: The Bossier Banner headed its report 'Arson and Judge Lynch,' called Solomon 'of a bad character,' hoped never again to chronicle 'Judge Lynch' but blamed 'legal quibbles and quirks.'
The Shreveport wire ran as 'Judge Lynch in Louisiana. A Horse Thief and Incendiary Hanged' (Savannah), 'Louisiana Lynch Law' (Richmond) and 'A Negro Hanged' (Knoxville).
The Claiborne Guardian summarized the facts without comment.
The Donaldsonville Chief's 'More Lynching' called the lynchers 'night-prowling jayhawkers' and 'cowardly murderers' and charged that they distinguished between a white and a Black prisoner.

versions.value: Fire Tuesday night (24 Jan.), keys taken 1-2 a.m. 'the same night,' body found 'yesterday morning' (25 Jan.)
Keys taken between 1 and 2 a.m., 26 January (Wyche's testimony as printed)

conflicts.note: The Banner's narrative, the Shreveport wire dated 26 Jan. ('yesterday morning') and the Claiborne Guardian ('the next morning') all place the hanging in the early hours of 25 January; the '26' in the testimony is likely a misprint.

versions.value: Hanged by 10 or 12 unknown men who took the keys

conflicts.note: The suicide version appears only in a secondhand French brief; the sworn inquest testimony and coroner's verdict support the lynching.
The local paper and the inquest testimony say mule; the wire's 'horse' is less specific.
Compatible descriptions of a hanging at the jail itself.
The deputy's sworn testimony is the better evidence.
The Chief's argument that the lynchers spared a white murderer rests on its description of Chapman; later Banner and wire reports call him colored.
